item.title: New Scientist: Explainer: What is El Niño?
item.description: Every few years, a disturbance in the Pacific Ocean is amplified by feedback mechanisms in the atmosphere, unleashing heat and extreme weather around the globe

item.title: New Scientist: The astonishing collective impact of household energy shifts
item.description: A subtle change in household power habits could eliminate the need to build new gas power plants, say researchers studying energy usage

item.title: Nature: Emissions after the Paris accord made Europe’s heatwaves more severe
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03035-w A heatwave in 2025 would have been one-third of a degree cooler without the greenhouse gases released since 2015.

item.title: New Scientist: Urban trees in south-east England can’t cope with the changing climate
item.description: In cities such as London, trees are already struggling with hot and dry summers. Botanists warn that we need to start replacing them with drought-adapted species

item.title: Nature: Lab-grown brain organoids: time for international oversight
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03048-5 Researchers in the field are right to focus on biosafety, ethics and the involvement of patient groups and the public.

item.title: New Scientist: Spectacular feathered dinosaur fossil shows bird-like adaptations
item.description: An exquisitely preserved fossil found in China shows that many anatomical features seen in birds also evolved independently in another group of dinosaurs

item.title: New Scientist: Why are so many animals moving to hotter places as the world warms?
item.description: We have long expected animals to move to cooler habitats as climate change bites, but it now appears that many are actually doing the opposite. What on earth is going on?

item.title: Nature: AI-powered medical devices must be tested in real-world settings
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03046-7 Tools that inform clinical decision-making require rigorous assessments equivalent to processes used to approve drugs and self-driving cars.

item.description: From Australia to California, the UK to Peru, turbulent weather is on the way

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02972-w A genus of soil-dwelling beetle discovered in Italy, and a glimpse at the wonders of the deep sea, in our weekly dip into Nature’s archive.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Old hearts ‘de-age’ in younger people
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03089-w Epigenetic 'clocks' suggest that transplanted organs adjust to the host's biological age. Plus, a new biography of Stephen Hawking and how sham societies are misleading star researchers.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Landmark bat study suggests they evolved in Europe
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03050-x A new project aims to generate chromosome-level genomes for all living bat species. Plus, AlphaFold has a new pandemic preparedness portal and security risks of AI.

item.title: New Scientist: Trustworthy science journalism is more essential than ever
item.description: As New Scientist celebrates its 70th anniversary, climate change, AI and misinformation have heightened the need for rigorous, sceptical reporting

item.title: Nature: The cost of lost labour on a warming planet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02971-x Researchers quantify the economic damage caused by climate-change-related heat stress on the global workforce.

item.title: Nature: China wants to build world-leading science journals — can it be done?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02759-z A new Chinese-owned journal Vita aims to compete with established journals.

item.title: Nature: A new chapter in targeting kinase enzymes in cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02776-y Inhibitors of tyrosine kinase enzymes have been a cornerstone in precision cancer treatments. Now, targeted protein degraders could reshape therapeutic options.

item.title: Nature: How to put people first in cyberspace
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02960-0 Digital technologies increasingly shape everyday life. Computer scientist Francine Berman tells Nature that stronger safeguards are required to protect the public interest.

item.title: ScienceDaily: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
item.description: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
item.description: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA’s Crew-13 could go from Florida to the ISS in under 9 hours
item.description: NASA and SpaceX could launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1, with the Dragon spacecraft reaching orbiting outpost less than nine hours after liftoff. Crew-13 will join Expedition 75 after teams complete a final round of intensive launch-readiness checks.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This suitcase-sized spacecraft could hear the universe before stars existed
item.description: CosmoCube will use the far side of the Moon as a shield from Earth’s radio noise to search for a faint signal from the universe before the first stars existed. The suitcase-sized satellite could reveal how the cosmic dark ages ended and how dark matter helped build the first galaxies.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
item.description: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
item.description: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
item.description: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications.

item.title: Nature: PhD training should encourage ethical dissent
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03053-8 PhD training should encourage ethical dissent

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03056-5 Biodiversity protection must include language preservation

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03054-7 Patents alone won’t unlock critical-mineral supply chains

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03055-6 Why AI-authorship debates miss a deeper shift in how scholarly knowledge is produced

item.title: Nature: AI can widen science — but only if institutions stop rewarding the already measurable
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02961-z Funders, journals and universities must reward the creation of new scientific terrain, not just the efficient mining of old ground.

item.title: Nature: Paid to peer review: firms are paying researchers to assess manuscripts for journals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02277-y Freelance peer-review jobs through third-party companies raise practical and ethical questions.

item.title: New Scientist: Scientists can’t stop using AI, even when forbidden from doing so
item.description: When scientists were asked to review papers for a conference without using AI tools, many of them ignored the request and used AI anyway

item.title: New Scientist: Our food system is vulnerable to El Niño, warns UK climate minister
item.description: Extreme weather could damage harvests worldwide, but the answer is more local food production, not stockpiling, Katie White said in an interview with New Scientist

item.title: New Scientist: Embracing the glitches in gravity could give us a unified theory of reality
item.description: Physicists have long struggled with their goal of making gravity a quantum force. A radical post-quantum approach might solve that problem – and clear up other cosmic mysteries, too

item.title: ScienceDaily: Diabetes study finds keeping blood sugar too steady may come at a price
item.description: People with diabetes reported better quality of life after days when their glucose stayed largely within a healthy range, even when levels fluctuated more than usual. The unexpected finding suggests that pursuing extremely tight glucose control may sometimes come with a hidden lifestyle burden.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
item.description: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. Decaf was associated with better learning and memory, while caffeinated coffee appeared to reduce anxiety and improve attention.

item.title: New Scientist: AI finds 3D shape that fills all space with a never-repeating pattern
item.description: A 3D shape that can tile 3D space, leaving no gaps and never forming a repeating pattern, has been discovered using an AI model. The researcher behind the findings, who has no academic background in the area, says his work has angered professional mathematicians

item.title: ScienceDaily: Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
item.description: Spaceflight may dramatically change the gut within weeks, causing bacteria to break down more protein as food moves more slowly through the intestines. The shift could help explain astronaut constipation and may have wider effects on health, making it an important concern for future missions to Mars.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
item.description: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.

item.title: ScienceDaily: James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time
item.description: JWST has revealed that young planetary systems lose their planet-building gas through a changing mix of powerful jets, molecular winds, and radiation-driven outflows. As the disks age and their gas disappears, giant planets face a shrinking window to build massive atmospheres.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Pomegranate compound improves heart function by up to 80% in study
item.description: A compound the body can make after eating pomegranates, walnuts, and some berries improved measures of heart function by up to 80% in animal models of a difficult-to-treat form of heart failure. Urolithin A helped stiff heart tissue relax and reduced scarring and abnormal enlargement. It also improved relaxation in engineered human heart tissue.

item.title: ScienceDaily: 160-million-year-old proteins show surprising power against superbugs
item.description: Scientists resurrected antimicrobial peptides from mammals that lived millions of years ago and found that some were more potent against drug-resistant bacteria than modern human versions. These evolutionary relics could provide new clues for designing treatments as antibiotic resistance becomes an increasingly serious threat.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Resetting the body clock could help the brain recover after stroke
item.description: Strengthening the body’s natural daily rhythms helped mice recover after stroke by improving the brain’s waste-clearing system and reducing lingering inflammation. The approach worked even when treatment began three days after the stroke, suggesting circadian-based therapies could eventually offer a new way to support long-term recovery.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
item.description: Measurements of ancient light from the cosmic microwave background suggest that the universe is remarkably flat. But that does not prove it is infinite, because the observable cosmos could be only a small patch of a much larger curved universe. Space could even be flat while wrapping around on itself in exotic ways.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
item.description: Scientists found that immune cells contributing to Alzheimer’s-related brain damage may be activated in lymph nodes outside the brain before traveling into the nervous system. Blocking this pathway in mice dramatically reduced neurodegeneration and preserved cognitive abilities, pointing to a potentially more accessible treatment target.

item.title: New Scientist: Why is this monster El Niño so strong?
item.description: Though the El Niño is still months from its peak, it is already breaking many records. Two main factors are behind how it became so powerful

item.title: Nature: Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02964-w Gene-editing techniques could soon allow researchers to replace entire genes and engineer complex cellular circuits — if the systems can be delivered safely into cells.

item.title: Nature: Vaping in childhood has bigger health risks than we’d thought
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02962-y Use of e-cigarettes makes it more likely that young people will experience mental-health disorders and take up smoking. Governments must act.

item.title: Nature: Stephen Hawking biography explores an ‘exceptionally clear, uncluttered mind’
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02959-7 An elegant account of the physicist’s unusual life story highlights the relationships that inspired him.

item.title: New Scientist: Can you hack your brain to be ultra-productive?
item.description: An endless stream of distractions, from email notifications to overlapping deadlines, can make focus slip away. Columnist Helen Thomson went hunting for neuroscience-backed ways to boost your productivity

item.title: Nature: China now leads the world in trials for next-gen CAR-T therapies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03004-3 China tests these therapies faster than the rest of the world but regulatory changes could slow them down.

item.title: Nature: Transplanted hearts adjust their biological age to that of their host
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03043-w Tracking the biological age of grafted organs suggests that donor pools could be expanded to boost organ availability.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
item.description: A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Atrial fibrillation patients saw 69% lower risk with common blood thinners
item.description: Direct oral anticoagulants cut the risk of serious clinical events by 69% in atrial fibrillation patients with an intermediate risk of stroke, according to the randomized SINGLE-AF trial. The benefit was driven mainly by fewer ischemic strokes, with no increase in major bleeding.

item.title: ScienceDaily: One CRISPR treatment cut “bad” cholesterol in half for a full year
item.description: A single dose of an experimental CRISPR therapy cut LDL cholesterol and triglycerides by about half in patients with difficult-to-treat lipid disorders. The reductions were still present one year later, with the highest dose lowering LDL by 52.5% and triglycerides by 47.8%.

item.title: ScienceDaily: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
item.description: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

item.title: ScienceDaily: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
item.description: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Why rheumatoid arthritis pain may persist even when inflammation is under control
item.description: Pain and fatigue in rheumatoid arthritis can persist even after inflammation improves, with depression, poor sleep, obesity, smoking, and chronic pain potentially helping sustain symptoms. Researchers say identifying these hidden drivers could prevent unnecessary medication changes and lead to more personalized treatment.

item.title: ScienceDaily: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
item.description: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists say house cats could help unlock better cancer treatments for humans
item.description: Scientists have mapped the genetics of cat cancer on an unprecedented scale and found surprising similarities with tumors in humans. The findings could help bring precision cancer treatments to cats while also revealing new clues about how human cancers develop and respond to drugs.

item.title: New Scientist: Blood test could gauge if a baby has a dangerous infection in 15 minutes
item.description: Feverish babies in hospital are often assumed to have a serious bacterial infection and are treated with antibiotics. But a test that gauges whether the infection is bacterial or viral, which tend to be milder, could prevent unnecessary drug use

item.title: ScienceDaily: A major risk of breast cancer screening may have been overestimated for decades
item.description: A new analysis suggests mammograms may lead to far less breast cancer overdiagnosis than some earlier studies indicated. Researchers reexamined all eight major randomized screening trials and accounted for differences in follow-up time, screening frequency, and screening after trials ended. Their results were consistent with an overdiagnosis rate below 5%, rather than estimates approaching 30% to 50%.

item.title: ScienceDaily: That fresh cleaning smell could be filling your home with nanoparticles
item.description: Researchers found that scented cleaners can react with ozone indoors to create billions or trillions of invisible nanoparticles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The pollution forms within minutes and, in some cases, may produce an inhaled particle dose comparable to or greater than standing near heavy traffic.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists may have misread a 2-billion-year-old clue about Earth
item.description: Scientists have found that a famous 2-billion-year-old chemical signature, once thought to record a massive global change in Earth’s carbon cycle, may instead have been produced by local magma, hydrocarbons, and methane-eating microbes. The discovery raises new questions about what was really happening as oxygen transformed the young planet.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists burned their own scrolls to unlock a 2,000-year-old mystery
item.description: Scientists discovered that tiny amounts of lead in ancient ink can make writing inside burned papyrus scrolls stand out dramatically in X-ray scans. The technique could help unlock lost Greek and Roman texts preserved by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius nearly 2,000 years ago.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Quantum computer simulates matter “popping into existence”
item.description: Scientists recreated a particle-forming process linked to the extreme physics of the early universe using a 13-ion quantum simulator. The breakthrough suggests quantum computers could eventually help researchers investigate how matter formed and evolved after the Big Bang.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Two astronauts who flew farther than anyone before are taking new NASA roles
item.description: Artemis II astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning to emeritus status at NASA after their historic journey around the Moon earlier this year. The pair will continue advising and mentoring NASA teams as preparations accelerate for Artemis III and future lunar missions. Their experience with Orion and deep-space operations could prove especially valuable as NASA works toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat
item.description: Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, activated calorie-burning brown fat in obese mice, revealing a potential metabolic effect beyond appetite suppression. If confirmed in humans, the finding could help explain the drug’s powerful benefits and inspire more comprehensive treatments for obesity and diabetes.

item.title: ScienceDaily: REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
item.description: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

item.title: ScienceDaily: The secret to growing food on Mars could be fungi
item.description: Scientists think beneficial fungi could help transform nutrient-poor lunar and Martian regolith into a material capable of supporting crops. By helping plants access nutrients and withstand harsh conditions, these microbes could someday make self-sustaining space farming more realistic.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Don’t toss cannabis leaves: They may contain rare compounds with medical potential
item.description: Scientists discovered rare flavoalkaloids in Cannabis leaves for the first time, along with dozens of other phenolic compounds that had never been reported in the plant. The findings suggest that Cannabis leaves, often discarded as waste, may contain a surprisingly rich source of potentially useful chemicals.

item.title: New Scientist: Virtual green spaces and classical music reduce blood pressure in hospital
item.description: Watching a river flow via a virtual-reality headset while listening to classical music seems to quickly bring people's blood pressure down from a dangerously high level in hospital

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discovered two bizarre new sea spiders that are “nightmare fuel”
item.description: Scientists discovered two strange new sea spider species in the Salish Sea, including a hairy-legged, red-eyed species that can groom itself with comb-like appendages. Another is frequently covered in tiny parasites, and researchers say many more undiscovered sea spiders may still be hiding in the region.

item.title: ScienceDaily: This “rare” autism-linked genetic disorder may be far more common than scientists thought
item.description: A major analysis suggests Phelan-McDermid syndrome, a genetic disorder closely linked to autism, may affect about 1 in 7,300 people and more than 45,000 Americans. Researchers warn that thousands of cases may remain hidden because genetic testing is often not performed, even as targeted treatments move into clinical trials.

item.title: ScienceDaily: CRISPR could help doctors attack blood cancer without destroying healthy cells
item.description: Researchers used CRISPR to remove CD33 from donor stem cells, potentially giving doctors a way to attack aggressive blood cancers without destroying the healthy cells patients need after a transplant. In a 30-patient trial, the edited cells successfully took hold and appeared to shield blood cells from a CD33-targeted cancer treatment.

item.title: ScienceDaily: CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
item.description: CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal
item.description: Researchers have shown that exotic quantum particles called non-Abelian anyons can perform the full range of operations needed for universal quantum computing. Using 54 qubits on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, they combined braiding and fusion to unlock capabilities that braiding alone could not provide.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Earth is tearing apart beneath the Pacific Northwest
item.description: Scientists have captured a subduction zone off Vancouver Island in the process of tearing itself apart, revealing that these massive tectonic systems may die piece by piece rather than all at once. The discovery could help explain ancient plate fragments, volcanic activity, and how hidden breaks beneath Cascadia may influence future earthquakes.

item.title: New Scientist: Is China catching up to the US and SpaceX on reusable rockets?
item.description: The next space race is not about making rockets faster, bigger or more capacious, but about reusing them reliably and cheaply. The US is well ahead, but can China catch up?

item.title: New Scientist: Anthropic’s discovery will, at best, be just another gene-editing tool
item.description: The AI company Anthropic has announced that its Claude large language model has discovered a system reminiscent of CRISPR, but that doesn’t mean the Nobel prizes will start rolling in, says Michael Le Page

item.title: New Scientist: Mathematician discovers rare eight-faced shape
item.description: It isn't easy to demonstrate that a new geometric shape can actually exist in the real world, but one researcher argues that the genus-3 polyhedron can

item.title: New Scientist: The first season of Heroes is almost perfect – here’s why
item.description: Starring the late Hayden Panettiere as the self-regenerating cheerleader who could save the world, science-fiction series Heroes first aired 20 years ago today. It might have gone downhill in subsequent seasons, but its first is still brilliant, says TV columnist Bethan Ackerley

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists gave worms magnetic bacteria. They lived 43% longer
item.description: A magnet-producing bacterium extended the average lifespan of C. elegans worms by more than 43% while helping protect their neurological and intestinal health. Researchers traced much of the effect to suppression of ferroptosis, a damaging form of cell death linked to iron buildup and oxidative stress.

item.title: ScienceDaily: “We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
item.description: A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
item.description: Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover an “impossible” cellular survival pathway that could help fight cancer
item.description: Scientists discovered a surprising backup system that lets mammalian cells make the essential amino acid cysteine even when the pathways once considered indispensable are disabled. The same survival mechanism may help cancer cells resist treatment, raising the possibility that shutting it down could make tumors easier to kill.

item.title: New Scientist: Copying others can help young orangutans build a broad diet
item.description: Orangutans spend more than eight years learning how to cope on their own, and now we have a clearer idea of how they work out which foods to incorporate into their diet

item.title: New Scientist: Dogs pay more attention to consonants than vowels when we speak
item.description: Hooking up dogs to non-invasive EEG monitors has helped identify exactly which component of human speech the animals are most attuned to

item.title: New Scientist: Backpack massages muscles when it detects they’re fatigued
item.description: A backpack consisting of electrodes, cables and a soft massage head kneads muscles in the back when it picks up on them being fatigued

item.title: New Scientist: Taking HRT in perimenopause may ward off cardiovascular disease
item.description: Hormone replacement therapies may reduce the risk of heart attacks and stroke, but the timing of when they are started could be critical

item.title: ScienceDaily: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
item.description: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
item.description: Researchers have shown that multiple time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, much like pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The coupling is carried by spin-polarized electrons, allowing time crystals separated by up to 40 micrometers to lock to a common frequency. The discovery reveals surprisingly long-range connections between these exotic spin systems and could help researchers develop future spin-based devices.

item.title: New Scientist: Skin patch that collects sweat could predict ovulation
item.description: A patch that measures levels of two reproductive hormones in sweat has shown promise for predicting ovulation in a small study

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
item.description: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
item.description: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
item.description: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

item.title: ScienceDaily: “We just need to go back” – Uranus’ moon Ariel may have hidden a 100-mile-deep ocean
item.description: Ariel, one of Uranus’ moons, may once have contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The finding, combined with similar evidence from Miranda, suggests the distant Uranian system could harbor multiple hidden ocean worlds.

item.title: ScienceDaily: These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
item.description: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected ways. The team also found large differences in iron abundance, a key ingredient in stellar winds and supernovae.

item.title: ScienceDaily: ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
item.description: A large Danish study found that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today more closely resemble their peers in the general population than those diagnosed 10 years ago. The shift suggests that rising diagnosis rates may partly reflect broader identification and changing diagnostic patterns, rather than only an increase in the underlying conditions.
